claims.text: The starting alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Cast HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
Uncoated HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxidation resistance for high-temperature use in air.
Extended high-temperature exposure in air embrittles uncoated HfNbTaTiZr and reduces its ductility below useful levels.
An Al-rich anti-oxidation surface coating can overcome the alloy's oxidation limitation.
Pack cementation can introduce the proposed Al-enriched surface layer on as-cast HfNbTaTiZr.
A post-cementation heat treatment will grow an external alumina scale.
The coating will form a dense, stable, and adherent alumina layer during exposure at 1000 °C in air.
The Al-rich coating will oxidize preferentially relative to the HfNbTaTiZr substrate.
The alumina layer will impede oxygen diffusion and lower oxygen permeability into the substrate.
Reduced oxygen ingress will reduce interstitial embrittlement.
The coating will significantly reduce oxygen pickup after exposure at 1000 °C in air for up to 100 hours.
Coated specimens will retain at least 8% tensile ductility relative to untreated specimens.
Coated specimens will retain a yield strength of approximately at least 160 MPa at 1000 °C.
The protective coating will preserve mechanical performance under tensile strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
Scale adherence at longer exposures or temperatures above 1000 °C is uncertain.
Thermal cycling and mechanical loading may cause coating spallation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows unchanged mechanical performance ('without degrading' or 'retention'), but the falsification rule rejects the hypothesis whenever coated specimens do not surpass uncoated specimens. Equal performance would therefore both satisfy the hypothesis and trigger falsification.
